title: Chapter 10: The Usual Arrangement
blurb: The east stair is mended by morning, but a clerk arrives with a tenant roll and an offer Ravi knows is real.

blocks.text: At midnight the two papers on the lobby board rewrote themselves while I watched. Copperplate came up through Greyfold's typing and through my own capitals like damp through paint, until the board held one sheet in a hand that wasn't mine and wasn't Walter's.

RULING. WO-1-001. EAST STAIR, CRACK. PUBLIC FLOOR. EVIDENCE OF CAUSE: PACKING NOTE, ADDRESSED BY GREYFOLD TO OCCUPANT, 6. COURIER RUN HISTORY, GREYFOLD DEPOT TO SERVICE-LIFT DOOR. WO-6-003, SLIP RED, FITTING UNDER GRADE. OCCUPANT OF FLOOR 6: NEARER LINK. GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS: DEEPER LINK. DISPUTE FAILS. ORDER STANDS ON GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS. OFFICER OF RECORD: I. TARRANT. STATUS: TRANSFERRED.
I'd won. Somewhere across the city a woman was trying to get up off her sofa with four storeys of brick in her legs, and I found I was talking to the stair.
"Sorry," I told it. "You're still cracked. That's the half I didn't listen to."

Kit was sitting on the bottom tread, wall side, helmet still on, phone in both hands. They'd come back at eleven to wait with me, because, they said, you don't leave a man alone with a notice board at midnight. The run history was still up on the screen: every Greyfold pickup in a column, the depot at one end and our service-lift door at the other.
"That's me," Kit said, and pointed at the line about the courier. "That's my bike in a ruling. Four stars. Docked one for the handwriting."
Dusty lay on his mat under the post table with his chin on his paws, and sighed. Down here that was all he had.

Walter had said it on floor 6 four hours before, and I'd heard the first half like a man hearing he'd passed. If I won, the stair stayed in her legs until her people fixed it. I hadn't heard the until. Winning hadn't put a spoonful of mortar back. The crack still ran up the stringer wall from the footing to floor 4, and at six o'clock a city inspector would put a torch on it whether Greyfold had lifted a finger or not.

And why would they? That was the theory I sat down with, on the step beside Kit, with the hot run's fever ticking in my face and my burnt knuckles stiff round a mug of cold tea. Greyfold wanted this stair to fail. A permit that only bites when a public floor fails its inspection is a permit that's hoping. Imogen could sit on her sofa until six with the weight in her legs, let the stair fail with her name on the sheet, and have what she came for. She could fix her legs afterwards, at her own pace, in a block that would be hers to knock down.
"She'll sit it out," I said.
Kit looked up the stairwell. "Would you?"
"I sat on a step all day."
"Yeah, but you were on the right side of it." Kit thought about it. "Different route. Same drop-off. Maybe."

At twenty to one, headlights swung across the lobby ceiling and stopped. A Greyfold van, and behind it a flatbed with a mixer strapped down and a stack of steel props. Four people got out in orange jackets. The one in front was a broad woman with short grey hair and a clipboard she didn't look at.
"Pask," she said. "Greyfold. You're the caretaker. Ms Tarrant says you'll take me up to beam two, and you'll know which collar."

"I will," I said. I said it before I'd decided whether I should, because a stair with a crew on it at one in the morning is a stair being mended, and I wasn't going to argue with that in a doorway. "Is she all right?"

Pask considered me. "She's on her sofa giving orders down the phone," she said. "Her legs aren't taking any. She sent you this." She held out an envelope. Inside was the carbon slip Kit had put into Imogen's hand that afternoon, folded once, with a pencilled note clipped to it: You'll need this to sign. I.
I stood there holding it longer than I needed to. She knew the rules better than I did. She'd known them all along.

The crew worked fast and didn't talk much. They propped the top flight off the floor-4 landing, mixed in the yard and pumped grout into the cored holes in the footing until it came out of the next hole along. Two of them cut slots across the crack every few courses up the stringer wall and bedded steel bars into them, the way you'd stitch a cut. I stayed out of their way and told them which treads Lou and Danny would come down at seven, so they'd have the wet work finished on that side first.

Then I took Pask up in the service lift. Dusty slipped in at my heels and sat in the corner like any dog. Pask watched me press 6, and the bead lit, and she breathed out through her nose as if she'd been told about this and hadn't believed it.
The boiler hall was hot, and my fever liked it there. The lodger saw the orange jacket before it saw me.
"IS THAT GREYFOLD?" it said, through every vent at once.
Pask went white and stayed where she was.
"It's Greyfold mending what Greyfold sent," I said. "It won't be long."
The furnace thought about that. "THEN I WILL WATCH."

Behind the gantry I put my palm on beam 2. The split collar was still soft, and the rod was still a finger low. Pask had a box of new collar nuts, plain brass, honestly stamped GRADE 1. We jacked the rod back up the finger it had dropped, and I took the old collars off one by one and dropped them into her box for her to take back to whoever had ordered them. Every new one I held at the fault before I threaded it. Grade one, every time. A public stair asks for grade one, and these were exactly what they said they were, which on this floor felt like a kindness.
"They're only grade one," Pask said, watching my face.
"I know," I said. "I believe them."

At five o'clock the props came out. I went down the stair to the third tread from the bottom, where the crack had started, and knelt on it with the slip on my knee. The stitched wall was dark with wet mortar all the way up. The grout in the footing had gone off hard. I read the slip twice, lips moving, and signed it at the fault.
WO-1-001. EAST STAIR, CRACK. PUBLIC FLOOR. CAUSE: GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS. REPAIRED BY: GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS. SIGNED OFF AT FAULT: R. ANAND. 05:02. STATUS: CLOSED. CREDITS: NIL.
I went down to the office to see it, because I needed to see it, and the line was black. Pask's phone went while I was coming back up. She listened, said "Right," and put it away.
"She's standing," she said.
The credits column hadn't moved. I didn't care, and I was surprised how much I didn't.

The inspector came at six on the dot: a tall city man in a long coat, with a torch, a crack gauge and a little hammer. He tapped his way up the stringer wall, shone the torch into the soffit of the top flight, and spent a long time on the footing. Then he wrote on his form, tore off a copy and gave it to me, and the copy said the east stair had passed.
I read it twice and put it in my shirt pocket, where it sat on top of the fever like a cold flannel.

Imogen came at twenty past, walking carefully, the way you walk on a floor you've been told is level and don't yet believe. She didn't come in. She stood on the front step, took the laminated permit off the oak door herself, pulled out the staples with her fingernails and folded it in half.

"Surrendered," she said. "I rang the city at six-oh-one. Greyfold holds nothing in Pellory Court as of this morning." She looked past me at the rear corridor, where the service lift was. "I shan't be needing your lift."
Whatever she'd been able to see on that brass panel, she couldn't see it now. I didn't know what to say to that, so I said the top hinge on the door wanted new pins, which she knew.
"You did that cleanly, Ravi," she said. "Go to bed."

Then she looked at me a second longer than the sentence needed, the way she had on this step on day seven, when she'd said my surname. I knew which other stair she was thinking of, because I was thinking of it too. She went down the steps one at a time, holding the rail, and the door rubbed the frame behind her.

I slept until two in the afternoon and woke hot. The stair was gone from my legs and the stair was mended, and I still had the hot run's fever and a set of striped knuckles to show for floor 6. One order, held since before the crack, and the weeks on its clock showing in my face.
At four I knocked on 4C. Mrs Wrobel opened the door with a tea towel over her shoulder, and Jurek's coat and slippers stood inside it the way they always did.
"I've got a question about the tap," I said.
"Ask."

I held out Jurek's washer on my palm. I'd carried it in my trouser pocket since the day she gave me the tap, next to Greyfold's counterfeit jumper, and the two of them had worn a hole in the lining between them.
"This was in it," I said. "I kept it back. I didn't know if the washer was part of what you gave."
"The tap was given," she said. "The washer was in the tap. Use it." She coughed, dry, into the tea towel. "This is a question? This is not a question."
I had the other question ready. Roll 4C. It sat on my tongue behind the washer, square capitals and all, and she stood there with her hand on the door, and I looked at the slippers and didn't ask it.
She went back into the kitchen and came out with a jar of beetroot soup with a saucer on top, and I took it, because I always take it.
"Tomorrow I go door to door," she said. "Old metal. Long used. Given. I know how it's done. You fit them new ones."
"I can do the doors myself."
"You can't do the stairs without falling asleep on them. I go."

That night I rode to floor 6 with the washer. The hot run's valve still had my old worn jumper in it, the one I'd refitted after Greyfold's failed. I stood in front of the pipe run with the heat coming off it into my face, the same heat that had lived in my blood for weeks, and I talked to it, because that's what I do on floor 6.
"I'll have you sound," I told it. "You first, and then every one of the rest of you, before I'm done with this floor. Same promise for all of you."

I turned the old jumper out, dressed the pin, and seated Jurek's washer on the plate. It was heavier in my hand than the tap had been. Heavier than Mr Tull's key. Sixty years of an old tram driver filling his kettle, and something in the brass knew about every one of them. I closed the valve on it, and the run stopped passing heat it hadn't asked for, and I signed the slip with my back against the gantry.

The fever went out of me like a tide going out. My knuckles stopped being hot, and the stripes on them were already fading. I sat on the gantry steps for ten minutes, cool for the first time in weeks, and the lodger roared something I took for approval.

Mrs Wrobel brought them down in a biscuit tin. Each piece was wrapped in newspaper with a flat and a number of years written on the outside in her slanting hand: a brass window stay from 3A with thirty-one years on it, a coat hook from 1B, two cupboard knobs from the Hendersons, a curtain rail out of 4A's bay window, and a pendulum bob off the kitchen clock in 2B, twenty-eight years, with LENT written under the number and underlined.
"He said lend," she said. "I wrote what he said."

I didn't think much of the underline. A pendulum that had swung for twenty-eight years in a lived-in kitchen was twenty-eight years of use whoever said what at the door. I took the next two orders on floor 6 that night, a weeping union on the return main and a beetle in the coal bunker, and carried an ache in both wrists like wet rope and an itch down the middle of my back that I couldn't reach. I fixed them with the window stay and the coat hook, signed them, and they lifted.

Each morning, before I slept, I went round the flats with the old super's SPARES box and fitted new: a new stay in 3A, new knobs for the Hendersons, a new hook in 1B. Mrs Quarry watched me do hers and told me the tenants' association had had a whip-round, on account of the stair, and that it was in my tip tin and I wasn't to argue. I didn't. Tips are tips.
On Thursday Kit turned up with a sack of honest coal on the bike trailer from the ropewalk yard, paid for out of the tin.

"Haulage is free," Kit said, before I could open my mouth. "Greyfold cancelled every furnace run I had. All of them, last night. I've got a hole in my week the shape of a boiler." They didn't look at me when they said it. Triple pay, every week, and their gran's damp flat down at Saltcote. "Don't. I know. Take the coal."

I took the coal. I carried it up myself, because Kit can't ride to 6 unless I take them, and I didn't want to take them yet. The lodger ate a shovelful and said HONEST in a voice that rattled the gantry.

The next night I took two more. The gantry lamp's circuit arced, and put a taste of pennies in my mouth and a twitch in my eyelid until one of the Hendersons' knobs, turned down into a terminal post, let me sign it off. The fanlight's draught came in under my ear and stayed there, an earache that made the whole left side of my head feel like a door left open. I'd shaped Mr Ferrabee's pendulum bob into a keep plate for the fanlight's catch, and it fitted sweetly. I held it at the fault before I screwed it home, and it was grade one in my hand. Plain new metal, near enough. All that swinging, and nothing in it.

I stood under the fanlight with the draught in my ear and thought about it the way I'd thought about Greyfold's stamp. The years were real. The use was real. What was missing was the word on Mrs Wrobel's newspaper. He hadn't given it. He'd lent it. And whatever reads brass on this floor had read that too.

I didn't fit it. I carried the earache down to 2B at eight in the morning with the bob in my hand and its keep plate filed into it, and said I was sorry about the shape, and explained that lent wasn't going to work.
Gil Ferrabee looked at the bob in my hand, and at me, and laughed. "It's a clock weight, mate. Have it. I mean it. Give, whatever the word is."
That night it was heavy in my hand, and the fanlight shut sweet, and the slip signed, and the earache went with it.
The book was waiting in the office when I came down to write the next cause.
CARETAKER: R. ANAND. GRADE: 2 (HANDYMAN). CREDITS: 21. HOLDING: 0. CERTIFIED: 5.

Handyman. A deputy for each order, if one would have me, and the order shared down the middle. I looked at the word for a long time and thought about Kit's hole in the week, and Mrs Wrobel's tin, and Gil laughing at me in his doorway, and I didn't ask anybody.

The last two went over two nights: the ash-pit door, seized on its hinge, which locked my jaw until I could hardly drink my tea, and the soot that crawled up the gantry legs, which made my eyes stream. 4A's curtain rail, thirty years of being drawn and opened, made a new hinge pin. The other Henderson knob, cut down into a ferrule, closed the joint the soot was crawling out of. I promised each of them the same thing, out loud, and kept it.

At ten past three one morning, a week after the ruling, I signed the last slip on floor 6, and my eyes stopped running. In the lift Dusty sat down in the open doorway, half on floor 6 and half in the car, and Walter looked up at me.
"Every slip on this floor honest," he said. "Nobody's managed that on six in a long while. Read seven's page in the office tomorrow. Not tonight. Tonight you sleep, son."
He got up and came in, and chose to say nothing more on the way down. In the lobby he was only a dog again.

In the office the floor-6 page had gone black from top to bottom, all but one line. WO-6-017 sat at the foot of it in its old colour, ABANDONED, with roll 4C in square capitals, and the book didn't count it.

FLOOR 6. WO-6-003. HOT RUN, REGULATING VALVE. CLOSED. WO-6-004. RETURN MAIN, WEEPING UNION. CLOSED. WO-6-005. COAL BUNKER, BORING BEETLE. CLOSED. WO-6-006. GANTRY LAMP, CIRCUIT ARCING. CLOSED. WO-6-007. FANLIGHT, DRAUGHT. CLOSED. WO-6-008. ASH-PIT DOOR, SEIZED. CLOSED. WO-6-009. GANTRY, CRAWLING SOOT. CLOSED. WO-6-017. FLUE BACKDRAFT. ABANDONED.
CARETAKER: R. ANAND. GRADE: 2 (HANDYMAN). CREDITS: 25. HOLDING: 0. CERTIFIED: 5, 6.

I went up the rear corridor to look, because I'm not made of stone. Above the 6 on the lift's brass panel, where there'd been a painted-over hole that morning, there was a brass button with a lamp behind a glass bead, and the lamp was lit.
The Clerk of Placements came the next afternoon.

I knew the title before I knew the man. For twenty-two years, every Friday, Mrs Wrobel had posted a letter to it. He was thin and grey and buttoned all the way up, with a folder under his arm tied with cotton tape, and when he came into the lobby it smelt like the office does when the book has been busy: carbon paper, and a little dust.
"Mr Anand," he said, as if we'd met. "Bastien Thewlis. Congratulations on the stair."
"It passed," I said. "Greyfold mended it."

"So I gather." He set the folder down on the post table, over Dusty's head, and untied the tape. "I've brought you something you ought to have had the day you took the post. Regrettably, it was held back."
It was a long ledger sheet folded in four, ruled in faded red. PELLORY COURT across the top. A line for every flat, with names in it I knew, and columns after the names I didn't.
"Every flat in this block was placed by my office," he said. "Under the usual arrangement. You've never needed to see it. You do now."
He turned it with one finger so I could read it the right way up, and laid the finger beside one line.
4C. J. WROBEL. 14 ABSORBED. DECEASED. A. WROBEL. 4 ABSORBED. CARRYING WO-6-017 (FROZEN).
I read it twice, lips moving.

WO-6-017. Flue backdraft. Dry cough. I'd stood over that line in the office with the fever in my face and read roll 4C as a lead joint on a flashing, and then as her flat. A list of names, I'd thought. And here was the list. Her cough was dry. Jurek had a cough like mine for years, she'd told me on the landing, with the soup. Fourteen. Whatever absorbed meant, it meant carrying a thing until there was nothing left of it to carry, and fourteen of them had been enough to finish a man who drove a tram for thirty-one years.
Somewhere above us a door opened and shut, and someone came down a flight, slowly, and stopped. Then the cough: dry, three times, the one she calls building cough, from the first-floor landing.

Thewlis didn't look up. He took two more papers from the folder and laid them side by side on the post table, squared to its edge. One was a licence in a card cover. The other was cream and heavy, with a space at the bottom for a signature and a dotted line for the date.

"A steward's licence," he said, "and a commission to go with it. It's the usual arrangement. Most of the keepers in this city hold one." His voice was very soft. "Sign, and you can move it off her tonight. Onto anyone you like."
I didn't pick them up. I didn't trust my hands to put them down again.
It was true. I didn't know how, but I knew it was true the way I'd known the tap was heavy. Somebody had put that order on her once, with a pen, in square capitals, and here on the table was a pen.
Mrs Wrobel coughed again on the landing. She didn't come down any further. She didn't say a word.

Dusty had got up off his mat and was standing by my knee, looking at the papers and then at me. On this floor he couldn't tell me anything. So I crouched down in front of the Clerk of Placements and talked to the dog anyway.

"You told me never take a raise from anyone but you," I said. "You never told me what to do about this. Those were your capitals on her line, weren't they? Is this what somebody put on a table for you?"
Dusty looked at me with a dog's face and said nothing, because down here he couldn't, and Thewlis waited, because he could.
